title: Surgeon at University of Maryland Removes Rare Spinal Tumour Through Patient's Eye Socket in World First
excerpt: Dr. Mohamed Labib led a team that removed a chordoma from a 19-year-old's spine via a transorbital approach, while a separate brain tumour was extracted through her nose — both firsts in neurosurgical technique.
body:
• A team at the University of Maryland Medical Center removed a rare spinal chordoma through a patient's eye socket — the first surgery of its kind
  • The same team also removed a brain stem tumour through the patient's nose using an endoscopic endonasal approach
  • Only about 300 chordomas are diagnosed in the United States each year, making this dual-tumour case exceptionally rare
  • The procedures, led by neurosurgeon Dr. Mohamed Labib, left no external scars and preserved major nerves and blood vessels

A First in Surgery

A team of neurosurgeons at the University of Maryland Medical Center (UMMC) has successfully removed a rare cancerous spinal tumour from a 19-year-old woman through her eye socket — the first time this transorbital approach has ever been used to reach the spine, according to the University of Maryland School of Medicine.

The patient, Karla Flores of Rosedale, Maryland, had two separate chordomas — slow-growing developmental bone tumours that arise from remnants of the fetal notochord. Only about 300 chordomas are diagnosed in the United States each year, and having two unconnected tumours was exceptionally rare.

"By going through the bottom of the eye socket, we were able to remove a tumor that otherwise would have been very difficult and very risky to address. We created a huge surgical corridor that enabled us to get in front of the spinal cord. It was a straight shot."

— Dr. Mohamed A.M. Labib, UMMC neurosurgeon

Three Surgeries, Zero External Scars

Flores required three separate procedures. Her brain stem tumour was addressed in two operations: surgeons first removed part of it through a traditional craniotomy, then extracted the remainder through her nose using an endoscopic endonasal approach — threading a thin, lighted endoscope with a camera through the nasal cavity to reach the skull base.

For the spinal tumour, Dr. Labib worked with Dr. Kalpesh Vakharia, UMMC's chief of facial plastic and reconstructive surgery. Vakharia carefully cut through the conjunctiva inside the lower eyelid without disturbing the eye, then removed the bottom of the eye socket and a portion of cheekbone to create a pathway. From there, Labib drilled through vertebral bone to access and remove the tumour.

After extraction, Vakharia rebuilt the eye socket floor using a titanium plate and reconstructed the cheek with bone from the patient's hip.

"We wanted to develop a surgical plan where there would be no external scars and it would be impossible to tell that the patient even had surgery."

— Dr. Kalpesh T. Vakharia, Chief of Facial Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery, UMMC

Pioneered on Cadavers

Dr. Labib developed the novel approach by practising extensively on cadavers in the Department of Neurosurgery's Skull Base 360° Laboratory. He called the eye socket "the third nostril" in preliminary research published in the Journal of Neurosurgery in October 2023, exploring new ways to access hard-to-reach skull base tumours.

The multidisciplinary team included neurosurgeons, skull base surgeons, facial plastic surgeons, and radiation oncologists. Flores also received proton radiation therapy to destroy any remaining cancer cells, and a separate spinal fusion to stabilize her neck.

The Endonasal Frontier

The endoscopic endonasal approach — removing tumours through the nose — has been transforming neurosurgery over the past two decades. Centres including the University of Pittsburgh, Stanford, UCLA, and Cleveland Clinic have refined the technique, which avoids the need for traditional craniotomy and significantly reduces recovery time.

The technique has particular relevance for medical centres in India, where institutions are increasingly adopting endoscopic approaches for complex skull base and brain tumour cases, expanding access to minimally invasive neurosurgery in a country with a growing burden of neurological disease.
nri_angle: Endoscopic neurosurgery techniques pioneered by teams like Dr. Labib's are increasingly adopted at Indian medical centres, expanding minimally invasive options.
